title: Seven Loaves, Half-Sight, and the Road of the Cross
summary: Jesus feeds four thousand people with seven loaves, refuses the Pharisees' demand for a sign, and rebukes his disciples for failing to understand the bread. At Bethsaida he heals a blind man in two stages. Near Caesarea Philippi Peter confesses that Jesus is the Christ, and Jesus begins to teach that the Son of Man must suffer, die, and rise, and that anyone who follows him must take up a cross.
story: This is the hinge of Mark's Gospel. For eight chapters the question has been who Jesus is, asked by crowds, demons, disciples, and a frightened king. Here Peter gives the right answer, and at once Jesus redefines it: the Christ must suffer. From this point the story turns toward Jerusalem, and each of the three predictions of the passion (8:31, 9:31, 10:33-34) is followed by the disciples' misunderstanding and Jesus' teaching on what following him costs. The chapter also closes the bread section that began in chapter 6. The second feeding, the argument about one loaf in the boat, and the blind man who sees only partly all press the same point: the disciples have eyes and do not yet see.
historical:
Caesarea Philippi lay about twenty-five miles north of the Sea of Galilee, at the foot of Mount Hermon beside one of the springs that feed the Jordan. The site had long held a shrine to the Greek god Pan, and Herod the Great built a temple there in honor of Augustus. His son Philip the tetrarch, who ruled the territories north and east of Galilee, rebuilt the town and named it for the emperor and himself, which is why it is called Caesarea of Philip. It was a thoroughly Gentile place, marked by pagan worship and imperial loyalty, and it is there, away from Jewish crowds, that Jesus asks his disciples who he is.

Dalmanutha, where Jesus lands after the feeding, is otherwise unknown; its location on the Sea of Galilee is uncertain, and Matthew's parallel names Magadan. Bethsaida was a fishing town at the northern end of the lake, in Philip's territory. The leaven of Herod refers to Herod Antipas, who had killed John (6:14-29), and the Pharisees had already conspired with Herod's supporters against Jesus (3:6). Crucifixion was Rome's punishment for slaves and rebels, carried out publicly, and a condemned man was often made to carry the crossbeam to the place of execution. When Jesus speaks of taking up the cross, his hearers would have pictured that walk.
cultural:
The second feeding is set, by the flow of the story since 7:31, in the Decapolis, a largely Gentile region. The number of baskets differs from the first feeding (seven here, twelve before), and so does the Greek word for basket: the first feeding uses a word associated with Jewish travelers, the second a larger basket used more widely. Many interpreters think the twelve baskets point to the twelve tribes of Israel and the seven to the nations, though that is an inference, not a statement of the text.

Leaven, a lump of fermented dough kept back to raise the next batch, was a common image for something small that spreads through the whole. At Passover Israel removed all leaven from the house, so it often stood for corruption. Messiah (in Greek, Christos) means anointed one, and in Jesus' day hopes for the Messiah centered on a king from David's line who would free Israel from its enemies, purify the land, and restore the kingdom. That is why Peter's confession needed immediate correction, and why a suffering and executed Messiah was, for most Jews, a contradiction in terms.
literary: Mark builds the chapter so that each part explains the others. The disciples' failure to understand the loaves (verses 14 to 21) ends with Jesus quoting the prophets' charge against Israel, “Having eyes, do you not see? And having ears, do you not hear?” (compare Jeremiah 5:21). Immediately a blind man is healed in two stages: first he sees people like trees walking, then everything clearly. The scene works as an acted parable of the disciples themselves. At Caesarea Philippi Peter sees partly: he knows the right title but not what it means. The second touch, clear sight, will come only through the cross. Verse 31 marks the turn with the words he began to teach, and the word must (Greek dei) signals divine necessity. The chapter ends with a series of sharp sayings on losing and saving life that apply the pattern of Jesus' road to everyone who follows him.

outline.t: Four thousand fed with seven loaves
The leaven of the Pharisees and Herod; the disciples' dullness
A blind man healed in two stages
The first passion prediction and Peter's rebuke

doctrines.note: Peter's confession, “You are the Christ,” is true, and Jesus accepts it, but he immediately fills the title with a new content: the Messiah is the Son of Man who must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise. The kingship is real, and the road to it runs through the cross.

The passion prediction says that Jesus' death is not an accident or a tragic defeat but something that must happen within God's purpose. Mark will explain the meaning of that necessity in 10:45, where Jesus gives his life as a ransom for many.

The Pharisees demand a sign and will not believe; the disciples have seen signs and still do not understand. Faith in this chapter is not produced by proof but by a second touch, an opening of eyes that comes from Jesus himself.

Following Jesus means denying oneself and taking up the cross. The kingdom's logic reverses ordinary values: whoever loses his life for Jesus and the gospel will save it, and no gain, even the whole world, is worth the loss of one's soul.

words.note: Christos, anointed one, the Greek translation of the Hebrew mashiach, messiah. In Israel kings, priests, and sometimes prophets were anointed with oil to mark them as set apart by God. By the first century the word had come to mean the promised king. Peter's use of it is the first time in Mark that a disciple names Jesus with the title from the book's opening line.

Dei, it is necessary, it must. Mark uses it here of the Son of Man's suffering, death, and resurrection. The necessity is not fate but the plan of God revealed in Scripture; Luke especially develops the word, and the risen Jesus will ask whether the Christ did not have to suffer these things (Luke 24:26).

Aparneomai, to deny, disown, or renounce. The same verb describes Peter's denial of Jesus in 14:30 and 14:72. Here Jesus asks disciples to deny themselves, to disown the self's claim to rule. Mark's readers would notice the irony: the one who refused to deny himself later denied his Lord.

Psuche, life or soul. The word covers both physical life and the person's inner self, and Jesus plays on the range: whoever tries to keep his life will lose it, and no gain can buy back a forfeited soul. English Bibles switch between life and soul in these verses, but it is the same Greek word throughout.

christ: Peter's confession states who Jesus is, and Jesus' teaching states what he came to do. He is the Christ, Israel's anointed king, and he is the Son of Man, the figure of Daniel 7 who receives an everlasting kingdom and who will come in his Father's glory with the holy angels. But before that glory he must suffer, be rejected by Israel's leaders, be killed, and rise after three days. The chapter joins what Peter wanted to keep apart, the crown and the cross. It also shows Jesus feeding hungry people in a desolate place, compassionate to a crowd that includes Gentiles, and patient with disciples who still see people like trees walking. The one who gives sight in two touches will open his disciples' eyes the same way, through the cross and the empty tomb.

hard.q: Is the feeding of the four thousand a second event, or a retelling of the feeding of the five thousand?
hard.a: The two stories are strikingly similar: a crowd in a desolate place, disciples who do not know where bread will come from, Jesus taking, giving thanks, breaking, and giving, everyone satisfied, and baskets of leftovers. Many critical scholars conclude that Mark received two versions of one tradition and included both. Others point out that the details differ consistently (five loaves and seven, two fish and a few small fish, five thousand and four thousand, twelve baskets and seven, a different word for basket, a Jewish setting and an apparently Gentile one, one day and three days), and that Jesus himself refers to both feedings as separate events in verses 19 and 20, a passage that makes no sense if there was only one. Matthew also includes both. Readers who take the Gospels as reliable history generally see two events, and note that repeating a sign in a different place with a different crowd was the kind of thing a teacher might well do. On either view Mark means the two feedings to be read together, as signs that Jesus feeds both Israel and the nations.

questions: Peter got the title right and the meaning wrong. What do you expect of Jesus that might need to be corrected by the cross?
The blind man saw partly before he saw clearly. Where in your understanding of God do you still see people like trees walking?
What would it look like, concretely, for you to lose your life for Jesus' sake this week, and what are you afraid of losing?
